Eggs of the Salmon-crested cockatoo (Cacatua moluccensis) are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that yields a developmental period of approximately 28.5 days [ab = approximately 28.5 days] before hatching. Newly hatched nestlings are altricial, exhibiting a wet weight at birth of roughly 16.7 grams [Wwb = roughly 16.7 grams], placing them at the lower end of the mass range reported for large-bodied cockatoo species. This modest neonatal mass underscores the substantial parental investment required during the early nestling phase, as chicks are entirely dependent on both parents for brooding and provisioning. The incubation period itself is comparable to that of other Cacatua species but is slightly prolonged relative to smaller-bodied parrots, a pattern consistent with the general allometric relationship between egg size and incubation duration across Psittaciformes. Field measurements indicate that eggs can vary somewhat in initial mass, but the mean hatchling weight remains remarkably consistent within clutches from a given breeding attempt.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the developmental trajectory of the nestling progresses through several well-defined milestones. Full cessation of parental feeding has been documented at approximately 77 days after hatching, a point that marks the transition toward nutritional independence. Prior to that, the fledgling achieves its first sustained flight at about 45 days after hatching [tx = about 45 days after hatching], a relatively early age given the substantial ultimate wet weight of 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams] attained by fully grown adults at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This adult mass, among the highest recorded for any cockatoo species, imposes considerable energetic demands on the growing chick. The fledging event itself is a critical juncture; the chick must be capable of sufficient flight to follow parents to foraging sites while still receiving supplementary feedings during the post-fledging dependency period. Comparative data from other large parrots suggest that the coordination between flight feather development and body mass gain is tightly regulated.

Reproductive maturity in Cacatua moluccensis is attained relatively late, with puberty recorded at 135 days after hatching [tp = 135 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This timing, however, does not coincide with immediate breeding activity; instead, the first successful reproductive event is typically deferred to approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching], as indicated by observational data from both wild and captive populations at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The delay between physiological puberty and actual first reproduction is often attributed to the time required for young birds to acquire a suitable nesting territory and to develop the pair-bonding behaviors essential for cooperative chick-rearing. Breeding pairs of this species exhibit strong site fidelity and typically return to the same tree cavity year after year. The single-egg clutch [N_R_i = single-egg clutch] laid during each breeding attempt represents an extremely conservative reproductive investment for a bird of this size, contrasting sharply with the larger clutches observed in many other parrot genera.

The maximum reproductive rate for the Salmon-crested cockatoo is constrained by both its clutch size and the frequency of nesting events. Females typically lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and the frequency of clutch production is approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year], reflecting the long period of parental care required by each nestling. This low annual fecundity is a defining characteristic of the species' life history strategy, which prioritizes high offspring survival through intensive biparental investment over the production of numerous young. The extended nestling and post-fledging dependency period, coupled with the substantial ultimate wet weight of 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams] that must be supported, makes each breeding event energetically costly for the adults. Such a life history pattern is typical of large, long-lived island endemics where adult survival is at a premium and environmental conditions are relatively stable.

Longevity records for Cacatua moluccensis indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 65.8 years [am = approximately 65.8 years] under favorable captive conditions maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a remarkable duration that places this species among the longest-lived of all psittaciform birds. This extreme lifespan is consistent with the slow life history syndrome observed in large-bodied parrots, characterized by delayed reproduction, small clutch sizes, and extended parental care. In wild populations on the islands of Seram and Ambon in Indonesia, the maximum lifespan is likely shorter due to predation pressure and habitat fragmentation, though precise field estimates remain scarce. The physiological mechanisms underpinning such longevity are thought to involve efficient cellular repair processes and a relatively low metabolic rate for a bird of this body mass. Ongoing captive breeding programs have provided valuable life history data, including confirmation that individuals can remain reproductively active well into their fifth decade of life, further attesting to the species' exceptional actuarial senescence schedule.
